extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and craftsmen/designers of architectural ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for designing architectural ornament: proportion, abstraction, and the use of color, with guidance on hierarchy, viewing distance, material, and compositional arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place ornament where it is useful and experienced
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no subject of street ornament so wisely chosen as the fountain, where it is a fountain of use; for it is just there that perhaps the happiest pause takes place in the labor of the day...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose ornaments that coincide with human pauses and uses (e.g., fountains where people stop and rest). Prefers ornament that serves or is encountered meaningfully rather than arbitrary decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary conditions: Proportion and Abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion and Abstraction are the two especial marks of architectural design as distinguished from all other [arts].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as the central, architecturally-essential qualities; other arts (painting, sculpture) may emphasize them differently. Use them as the organizing principles when imitating natural forms in architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of supremacy (one principal member)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever Proportion exists at all, one member of the composition must be either larger than, or in some way supreme over, the rest. 'Have one large thing; and several smaller things, or one principal thing and several inferior things, and bind them well together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid composing of equal things only (symmetry without proportion). Determine a principal mass by size, office, or interest (examples: centre of a west front; a spire with pinnacles). Anti-patterns: towers equal to and overpowering the centre; pinnacles without a spire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equality and vertical equal divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no proportion between equal things. They can have symmetry only, and symmetry without proportion is not composition... all vertical divisions of this kind are utterly wrong; worst into half, next worst in the regular numbers which more betray the equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horizontal symmetry/balancing can be allowable, but vertical equal division (e.g., cutting columns or spires in half by ornament bands) is generally a mistake. Prefer unequal, progressive divisions vertically; use three parts vertically rather than equal halves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion requires at least three terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion is between three terms at least... it is not enough... to divide a building unequally; it must be divided into at least three parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On a large scale, vertical elevation often works best in three parts; horizontal extent often in five; small-scale details may use more but avoid exceeding clarity (architectural recommendation: ~3 vertical, ~5 horizontal). Use pinnacles + spire + tower as an example of three-term relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of symmetry and proportion to axes
rubrics_metrics.description: The connection of Symmetry with horizontal, and of Proportion with vertical, division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry primarily for horizontal divisions (balance at the side) and use proportion to organize vertical hierarchies (avoid vertical equality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy within mouldings and details
rubrics_metrics.description: In mouldings of fine work (example from Rouen) there are multiple orders; the leaf moulding is much the largest, next the outer roll, then the innermost roll, with capitals and shafts scaled to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mouldings with a clear, graduated scale (arithmetical progression of sizes where appropriate). Each roll or order should have its own shaft and capital proportioned to its visual effect. Avoid misarrangement of central shafts that creates awkward heavy lateral members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graduated alternation and alternation omissions for lightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternation (e.g., omitting one of a double group on the other side of the moulding) gives playful lightness; careful alternation of sizes prevents loss of detail in recesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ alternation and deliberate omissions in repetitive ornament to reduce heaviness and introduce visual play; adjust inner rolls and fillets to avoid loss of form in deep recesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion in nature as an illustration, not a formula
rubrics_metrics.description: All beautiful proportions are unique, they are not general formulæ... proportions are as infinite... as possible airs in music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to teach exact ratios as universal formulas; use natural examples (plant stems, leaf ribs) as inspiration for subtle diminishing proportions, but expect unique solutions rather than fixed numeric rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction: express only necessary qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: All art is abstract in its beginnings; it expresses only a small number of the qualities of the thing represented... the abstraction properly consists only in a due expression of their subordination, an expression varying according to their place and office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When imitating natural forms in architecture, select and express only the characteristics needed for the intended place and effect. Avoid unnecessary detail that does not serve compositional subordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary degree of abstraction by distance, position, and formality
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction is influenced by nearness to the eye and by the formality of the whole; nearer elements may be more fully modelled, distant ones more abstract. Proportion completeness should be proportioned to the formality of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design with viewing distance in mind: ornaments close to the eye can be cut more fully and with higher finish; those intended to be seen from distance should be simpler and more abstract. Also match the degree of finish to the importance and formality of the element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design process: severe abstraction first, then selected finish
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a safe manner to design all things at first in severe abstraction, and to be prepared, if need were, to carry them out in that form; then to mark the parts where high finish would be admissible, to complete these always with stern reference to their general effect, and then connect them by a graduated scale of abstraction with the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with abstracted designs to secure compositional integrity; only afterwards choose and execute areas for high finish, ensuring they serve the overall composition and are connected by graduated levels of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of excessive completion of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect sculpture as part of architecture is dangerous: the moment the architect allows himself to dwell on the imitated portions, there is a chance of his losing sight of the duty of his ornament... his architecture has become a mere framework for the setting of delicate sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting ornamentary sculpture dominate and reduce architecture to a frame. Treat imitative ornament as the extreme of grace in language—valuable but not to be obtained at cost of purpose, meaning, force, or conciseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate only natural and noble subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Never imitate anything but natural forms, and those the noblest, in the completed parts... the degradation of Renaissance ornament was due not to naturalism but to its imitation of ugly, i.e., unnatural things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict detailed, fully finished imitation to noble natural objects (animals, flowers). Avoid using crude or unnatural motifs; choose subjects that maintain dignity and avoid decorative trivialities that degrade the architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture requires color; use natural stone tones
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot... consider architecture as in any wise perfect without color... the colors of architecture should be those of natural stones; partly because more durable, but also because more perfect and graceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept color as an attribute of architectural reality and prefer natural stone hues over painted tonality applied by unskilled hands. If painting is used, expect the skill of a true painter; otherwise prefer noble materials whose hues suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural color should be independent of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be visibly independent of form. Never paint a column with vertical lines, but always cross it... Never give separate mouldings separate colors... vary both the ground and the figures with the same harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat color as a separate system from form—apply variegation across broad surfaces and avoid simply following moulding lines. Do not typically color each moulding a separate tone; use harmonious variation of ground and figures so color and form are two distinct but compatible systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place variegation on broad surfaces; simplify color when form is rich
rubrics_metrics.description: The best place for color is on broad surfaces, not on the points of interest in form... it is a safe rule to simplify color when form is rich, and vice versa; and I think it would be well in general to carve all capitals and graceful ornaments in white marble, and so leave them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply variegated color boldly on flat walls and large shafts; keep capitals and delicate mouldings simpler (prefer white marble or neutral treatment). Balance color complexity and formal richness to avoid visual discord.
